Makkan, and it has forty-five or forty-six verses [it was revealed after Surah al-Naba']. In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

God, glory be to Him, swears by the groups of angels who pull out souls from bodies, and by those who draw them out gently (nashat), meaning they bring them out, from the expression "nashata al-dalw min al-bi'r" (he drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out, and by those who glide swiftly through their passage, meaning:

they hasten and so outstrip others to what they were commanded, and so they manage some affair of the servants that benefits them in their religion or their worldly life, as they were ordered. "Gharqan" means drowning, i.e., in the pulling out, meaning they pull the souls from the farthest parts of the bodies, from their fingertips and nails.

Or he swears by the horses of the raiders, which pull at their reins, so that the reins sink into the pulling because of their long necks, since they are Arab horses (kharab).

"Those who leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war," from your saying "thawr nashit" (an active bull) when it goes out from one land to another. "Those who glide swiftly in their running, so they outstrip to the goal and so manage the matter of victory and triumph." The attribution of the management to them is because they are among its causes. Or he swears by the stars that pull from east to west. Their drowning in the pulling means: that they traverse the whole sphere until they descend to the farthest west. "And those that leave one zodiac sign for another, and those that glide through the sphere among the planets, so they outstrip and manage a matter of the science of computation (ilm al-hisab)."

It has been said that "al-nazi'at" are the hands of the raiders, or their selves, which pull the bows with the drawing of arrows. "And those that loosen the ropes" [[His statement "tunshitu al-awhaq" (loosen the ropes): they are the tethers of livestock, as reported in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari). (Ayn)]]. The object of the oath is omitted, and it is "you will surely be resurrected," indicated by what follows it of the mention of the Resurrection. "On the day the earth quakes" is in the accusative, governed by this implied verb. "Al-Rajifah" is the event at which the earth and the mountains quake, and it is the first blast:

it is described by what occurs at its happening. "Tatba'uha al-radifah" means the event that follows the first one, and it is the second blast. It is permissible that "al-radifah" be from His saying, exalted is He: "Say: perhaps some of what you are hastening will come close behind you" (27:72), meaning the Resurrection, which the disbelievers hasten, deeming it far off, and it is "close behind them" because of its nearness. It has also been said that "al-rajifah" is the earth and the mountains, from His saying "on the day the earth and the mountains quake" (73:14), and "al-radifah" is the sky and the stars, because it splits and its stars scatter upon that. If you ask: what is the position of "tatba'uha"? I say: it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "on the day of quaking, the quake is followed by the follower." If you ask: how did you make "on the day the earth quakes" a time-frame for the implied verb "you will surely be resurrected," when they are not resurrected at the first blast? I say: the meaning is: you will surely be resurrected in the wide time in which both blasts occur, and they will be resurrected during some portion of that wide time, which is the time of the other blast. What indicates this is that His saying "tatba'uha al-radifah" was made a circumstantial clause of "al-rajifah." It is also permissible that "on the day the earth quakes" be governed by what is indicated by His saying "hearts on that day will be trembling" (79:8), meaning: on the day the earth quakes, hearts will have trembled, "wajifah" meaning intensely agitated; "al-wajib" and "al-wajif" are brothers in meaning. "Khashi'ah" means humbled. If you ask: how is it permissible to begin with an indefinite noun? I say: "qulub" is in the nominative as the subject, "wajifah" is its attribute, and "absaruha khashi'ah" is its predicate, so it is like His saying: "A believing slave is better than a polytheist" (a verse-like construction in the grammar of such utterances).

If you ask: how is it correct to attribute "absar" (sights) to "qulub" (hearts)? I say: its meaning is the sights of their owners, as evidenced by His saying "they say." "Fi al-hafirah" means in the original state, meaning life after death. If you ask: what is the reality of this word? I say: it is said: "rajaa fulan fi hafirihi," meaning he returned on the path on which he came, which he had dug, i.e., he left an impression on it by walking on it: he made the traces of his feet into digging, as it was said: "hafarat asnanuhu hafran" when the eating left its mark on the roots of his teeth [[His statement "the eating left its mark on its roots" (athar al-akal fi asnakhiha): in al-Sihah, "asnakh al-asnan" are their roots. (Ayn)]], and "the trench dug in the rock." It has also been said: "hafirah," as it is said: "a pleasing life" (69:21), meaning attributed to digging and to pleasing, or like their saying "your day is fasting." Then it was said of one who was in a matter, then went out from it and returned to it: "he returned to his hafirah," meaning his path and his original condition. He said:

"Is it a return to the original state, with baldness and graying hair?
God forbid it, from folly and shame."

[[Recited by Ibn al-A'rabi. The hamzah is for denial. "Al-hafirah" originally means the path dug by travel, so calling it "hafirah" is a rational metaphor, or it is in the sense of the relative: possessing digging; then it was used for every state you were in and then returned to. It is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall I return to the original state," i.e., in my first way of youth and childhood. Or it is by omission of the preposition, meaning: "Shall I return to it?" "Al-salf" is the receding of the hair of the forehead, and it is prevalent in old age. "Ma'adh" is a verbal noun in the accusative governed by an implied verb. "Al-safah" is ignorance and levity.]]

He means: a return to the original state. It has also been said: "the currency at the hafirah," meaning at the original state, which is the transaction.

It is the decayed, hollow bone through which the wind passes so that a hum is heard from it. "Idhan" is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, its estimate being: "When we are bones, shall we be returned and resurrected? That would be a losing return," attributed to loss, or whose companions are losers. The meaning is: if it is true, then we are losers for denying it, and this is their mockery. If you ask: to what is His saying "it is only a single shout" connected? I say: it is connected to an implied verb whose meaning is: do not regard it as difficult, for it is only a single shout, meaning: do not think that return is difficult for God, mighty and majestic, for it is easy and simple in His power; it is nothing but one cry [[Mahmud said: "If you say: how is it connected to what precedes it? He answered that they denied the repetition..." Ahmad said: how fine is the easing of the matter of repetition by His saying "zajrah" in place of "sayhah" (cry), since the "zajrah" is lighter than the "sayhah," and by His saying "wahidah," i.e., not in need of a second, and this establishes for you what you answered from the question arising at His saying "when the trumpet is blown with a single blast" (69:13), where it was asked: how is it single when they are two blasts? Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said:

"And a sahirah in which the mirage in the morning covers
its horizons, which I crossed wrapped in a veil."

[[By al-Ash'ath ibn Qays. "Al-sahirah" is the white land, because the mirage flows over it so that it resembles the wakeful eye, because of the brightness of its whiteness and the flow of its water, unlike the drowsy one (na'imah). Or it is described with wakefulness, because the traveler in it is awake and does not sleep for fear of destruction, so it is a rational metaphor. He says: how many a desert the day covers with a mirage resembling the saddle-cloth of a horse; "al-nahar" is applied to the mirage, and to the young of the bustard, and both meanings are valid. **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 79, verses 15–26:**

﴿Go﴾ is said with the sense of "say" implied. In the reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), it is ﴿an idhhab﴾ (that go), because calling (*nida'*) carries the meaning of saying.

﴿Are you willing to…?﴾ and ﴿Are you inclined to…?﴾ are like saying: "Are you inclined to it?" (*hal targhab fihi*) and "Are you inclined toward it?" (*hal targhab ilayhi*).

﴿That you purify yourself﴾: that you cleanse yourself from polytheism. The people of Medina read ﴿tazakka﴾ with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters).

﴿And I would guide you to your Lord﴾: I would guide you to the knowledge of God, alerting you to Him so that you know Him, ﴿and you would fear﴾, because fear is not possible except through knowledge. God the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾, that is, those who know Him. Fear is mentioned because it is the foundation of the matter: whoever fears God, all good comes from him, and whoever feels secure becomes bold in every evil. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever fears sets out early, and whoever sets out early reaches the destination."¹

He began his address with a question whose meaning is an offer, as a man says to his guest: "Would you like to stay with us?" He followed it with gentle speech to summon him by softness of words and to bring him down from his arrogance through conciliation, as he was commanded in His saying: ﴿Speak to him gently﴾, and the verse.

﴿The greatest sign﴾: the transformation of the staff into a serpent, because it was the premise and the principal matter, while the other (the hand) was secondary to it, since he used to shield himself with his hand from it, so it was said to him: ﴿Put your hand into your pocket﴾. Or he meant both together, but made them one, because the second was as if part of the first, being subordinate to it.

﴿But he denied and disobeyed﴾: he denied Moses and the greatest sign, and called them a magician and magic; and he disobeyed God the Exalted after he knew the truth of the command and that obedience had become binding upon him.

﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾: that is, when he saw the serpent, he turned away in terror. ﴿Striving﴾: he hastened in his walk. Al-Hasan said: "He was a hasty, light-minded man." Or: he turned away from Moses, striving and exerting himself in plotting against him. And it may be intended: "Then he came forward, striving," as you say: "So-and-so came forward to do such-and-such," meaning: he began to do it. So ﴿turned away﴾ is placed in the position of ﴿came forward﴾, so that he would not be described as having advanced.

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: his first utterance was ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾, and the last was ﴿I am your most high lord﴾.

﴿An exemplary punishment﴾: this is an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkid*), like God's promise and God's dye (*ṣibgha*); as if it were said: God made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first (life), and the *nakal* means *tankil* (exemplary punishment), like *salam* meaning *taslim*. That is, drowning in this world and burning in the Hereafter.

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: the *nakal* of his two utterances, the last being ﴿I am your most high lord﴾ and the first being ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾. It was also said: there were forty years between the two utterances.

The Great Calamity is the calamity that overwhelms all other calamities, meaning that it rises above and prevails over them. Among their proverbs: "The valley flowed and overwhelmed the villages." It is the Resurrection, because of its overwhelming every terrifying event. It was also said that it is the second blast of the Trumpet. It was also said that it is the Hour in which the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire.

﴿The day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitution for "when it comes." That is, when he sees his deeds recorded in his book, he will remember them, though he had forgotten them, as in His saying: ﴿Allah has enumerated them, though they forgot them﴾.

In "what he strove for," the "what" (mā) is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). ﴿And Hell is brought forth﴾: it is made manifest. Abu Nahik recited "wa-burrizat" (with emphasis on the verb). ﴿For whoever sees﴾: for all those who see, that is, for everyone. The meaning is that it will appear in a plain and uncovered manifestation, which all the inhabitants of al-Sahirah (the surface of the earth where people are gathered) will see, as in the saying: "The dawn has become clear to the one with two eyes," meaning to everyone who has sight. This is an image for a matter that has been uncovered and that is hidden from no one.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "li-man ra'ā" (for whoever saw). Ikrimah recited "li-man tarā" (for whoever sees). The pronoun refers to Hell, as in His saying: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾. It was also said that the address is to you, O Muhammad: "for whom you see."

Fa-ammā (فَأَمَّا) is the answer clause (jawab) here, meaning: "Then, when the Great Calamity comes, the matter is as such." The meaning is: "Then indeed Hellfire is his abode," just as you say to a man, "Lower the gaze" (ghuḍḍ al-ṭarf), meaning "your gaze." The alif and lam (al-) are not a substitute for the possessive (iḍāfa). Rather, since it is known that the transgressor is the owner of the abode, and that a man does not lower the gaze of anyone other than himself, the possessive was dropped, and the definite article entered "the abode" (al-ma'wā) and "the gaze" (al-ṭarf) for definiteness, because both are known. And huwa (هِيَ) is a separator (faṣl) or a subject (mubtada').

﴿They ask you, "When is its appointed time?"﴾ Its *mursa* (its settling), that is, its establishment: they meant, "When will God establish it, fix it, and bring it into being?" It is also said that *ayyan* means its final limit and resting place, just as the *mursa* of a ship is its resting place, where it comes to rest. [[Mahmud said: "*Mursaha* means its resting place... etc." Ahmad said: In this there is an indication of the heaviness of the Day, like His saying ﴿and leave behind them a heavy day﴾. Do you not see that they use *irsa'* (settling) only for what is heavy, like a ship's anchor and the settling of mountains?]]

﴿What are you in it?﴾ means: in what are you, that you should mention its time to them and inform them of it? [[Mahmud said: "The meaning of *fima anta* is: in what are you, that you should mention its time... etc." Ahmad said: There is a problem with this interpretation, for another verse rejects it: His saying ﴿They ask you as if you were eager to know about it﴾, meaning that you are not concerned with asking about it and do not care about it, whereas they ask you as one who is eager asks about a thing, that is, one who asks about it much. Therefore the first interpretation is more correct.]] In other words: you are not in any way concerned with mentioning its time to them or making its timing clear.

It is related from ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) continually mentioned the Hour and asked about it until this was revealed. [[Al-Isḥāq recorded it in his Musnad, and Ibn Mardawayh from his chain: "Ibn ʿUtba informed us, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from her," with this wording. al-Ṭabarī related it from Yaʿqūb, from Ibrāhīm, from Ibn ʿUtba, similarly. al-Ḥākim said after he recorded it through Ibn ʿUtba: "They (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) did not record it, because Ibn ʿUtba used to transmit it as mursal (with a missing companion)." Ibn Abī Ḥātim said from Abū Zurʿa: "The sound version is mursal." ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded it from Ibn ʿUtba as mursal, and al-Dāraquṭnī said: Ibn ʿUtba transmitted it once with a complete chain and once as mursal.]] Accordingly, this is a statement of wonder at how often he mentioned it, as if it were said: "In what occupation and concern are you, by mentioning it and asking about it?" The meaning is: they ask you about it, and out of your eagerness to answer them, you continually mention it and ask about it.

Then He said: ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, that is, the final limit of its knowledge: He has not given knowledge of it to any of His creatures.

It is also said that *fima* is a denial of their question, meaning: "Why this question?" [[Mahmud said: "It is also said that *fima* is a denial of their question, i.e., why this question... etc." Ahmad said: According to this, one should pause at His saying *fima* in order to separate the two statements.]] Then it was said:

﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, your sending (as a messenger) is not for mentioning it. You are the Seal of the Prophets and the last of the Messengers, sent "in the breezes of the Hour" [[His saying "in the breezes of the Hour": in the *Ṣiḥāḥ* (of al-Jawharī), "*nasam al-rīḥ*" is the first of the wind when it comes gently before it blows strongly. From the hadith, "I was sent in the breezes of the Hour," meaning: when its beginnings started and came near.]], so you have mentioned it and given a sign of its signs. This is enough for them as evidence of its nearness and imminence and of the obligation to prepare for it. There is no point in their asking about it. ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, you were not sent to inform them of the time of the Hour, whose knowledge is of no benefit to them; rather, you were sent to warn of its terrors whoever will be moved by your warning to fear it.

It has been read as *mundhir* with tanwin (nunation), which is the original form, and with the *idafa* (genitive construction), which is a lightening. Both are suitable for the present and the future. If the past is intended, only the *idafa* is possible, as when you say, "He warned Zayd yesterday." 

﴿As if they had not remained (in the world, or in the graves) except for an evening or its morning.﴾ 

If you ask: how is the *duha* (forenoon) validly attached to the *ʿashiyya* (evening)? I answer: because of the connection between them, since both occur in one day. If you ask: why not say "except an evening or a morning," and what is the benefit of the *idafa*? I answer: it indicates that the duration of their stay was as if it did not reach a full day, but only an hour of it, its evening or its forenoon. Since he omitted "day," he attached it to its evening. This is like His saying ﴿They did not remain except an hour of a day﴾.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the sūra *al-Nāziʿāt* will be among those whom God holds back in the grave and on the Resurrection until he enters Paradise, for the duration of an obligatory prayer."
